title: Acharei Mot: the goat to Azazel (Leviticus 16:21–22)
hook: wrongs are confessed over a goat sent into the wilderness

segments.voice: Yesterday in Acharei Mot, even the high priest could not enter at all times. Your line was not at all times. Did you keep one limit last night? Today, the strangest moment of the holiest day. Day four hundred seven.

Scapegoat. In English it means the one who takes the blame for everybody. The intern blamed for the server crash. The kid blamed for the broken lamp. It's become a word for unfairness. But it started as something else entirely, in Leviticus 16. On Yom Kippur, two goats stand before the high priest. As alike as possible, the rabbis said, in look, in size, in price. Lots are drawn. One is marked for God. And the other is marked with a word nobody has ever fully explained.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TAKES THE BLAME.` → `TWO GOATS, AS ALIKE AS POSSIBLE.` → `ONE FOR GOD, ONE FOR AZAZEL.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. The high priest lays both hands on the head of the living goat and confesses over it all the wrongs of the people. Then a man appointed for the job leads it into the wilderness, carrying those wrongs, the text says, to a land cut off. Second, the word. The lot says: for Azazel. What is Azazel? Honestly, nobody knows for certain. The Talmud reads it as the name of a place: the hardest, steepest of mountains, a cliff. Rashi follows that. Others, ancient and modern, read it as the name of a wilderness being. Commentators have argued about it ever since, and the text doesn't settle it. Third, how scapegoat got into English. When William Tyndale put the Torah into English in 1530, he read the Hebrew as ez ozel, the goat that goes away, and wrote scapegoat: the goat that escapes. So the English word comes from one translator's reading of a puzzle. Fourth, what it meant to the people. The Mishnah describes a crimson thread tied to the goat, and records a tradition that when the goat reached the wilderness, a crimson thread tied at the sanctuary turned white, and the people took it as a sign of forgiveness. Notice what the ritual is not. Nobody blames the goat. It isn't punished for being bad. It's a vehicle: the wrongs are named out loud, then carried far away. Send it away.
screen: `BOTH HANDS ON ITS HEAD.` · `AZAZEL: A CLIFF, OR A NAME?` · `TYNDALE'S SCAPEGOAT.` · `THE THREAD TURNED WHITE.` · then, large: `SEND IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one wrong down and tear it up. Find a scrap of paper. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've done that you're still carrying. Not your whole life. One thing. Write it down in a few words, plainly, the way the high priest named the wrongs out loud. Read it once. Then tear it up, small, and throw it away. Tomorrow we'll talk about what tearing it up can't do. For today, let it go into the wilderness. The bell holds the time.
Azazel. The mysterious destination of the second goat on Yom Kippur, carrying the people's wrongs into the wilderness. A cliff, or a name: the sources differ.
Your line: send it away. Today, when the wrong you tore up comes back to mind, picture it walking off into the wilderness. Day four hundred seven.

howItsDone: The goat ritual ended with the Temple; on Yom Kippur the Avodah service retells it, and on Rosh Hashanah many Jews practice tashlich, saying verses beside flowing water, and some cast crumbs into it, as a picture of sending wrongs away.

fork.reveal: both hands on its head, the wrongs confessed aloud, then it's led into the wilderness, to Azazel.

original.note: Hebrew: the word on the second goat's lot (Leviticus 16:8). its meaning is debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scapegoat, someone blamed unfairly.
what it means: a goat that carried the people's named wrongs away, without being blamed itself.
what a scholar hears: Yoma 67b reads Azazel as a hard, steep mountain; others read a proper name; Tyndale's 1530 'scapegoat' reflects ez ozel, the goat that departs.

notes: Mishnah Yoma 6:1: the two goats should be alike in appearance, height and value; confirm.
Yoma 67b and Rashi: Azazel as a strong, hard mountain/cliff. The 'wilderness being' reading (e.g., 1 Enoch; hinted at by Ibn Ezra and discussed by Ramban) is stated without naming sources.
Crimson thread turning white: Mishnah Yoma 6:8 records it as a tradition ('some say'); also Yoma 39a. The script says 'records a tradition'.
Practice previews tomorrow (Mishnah Yoma 8:9) without teaching it.

Editor review (y2 judaism 407–425): Tyndale wrote 'scapegoat' (scape = escape), not 'escape goat'; fixed teach, screen head, match and myth. Hook opener no longer tells the listener what they've used; 'for centuries' softened; crimson thread placed at the sanctuary and framed as a sign people took; tashlich described without overstating crumbs.
